To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

changes in self-reports of emotion may be detected with greater sensitivity when (1) discrete emotions are measured, rather than by a combined measure of negative emotion, and (2) participants are asked to report how they feel during, rather than immediately after, an emotional manipulation.

changes in selfreported negative emotion can be detected more sensitvely when discrete emotions are reported rather than by either the PANAS Negative Affect scale or a measure created using discrete emotions and when participants are instructed to report how the y felt during an emotioneliciting event versus afterwards.

a) self-reports of discrete emotions can be more sensitive than self-reports of global negative affect; b) self-reported discrete emotions are sensitive to emotional change, and c) self-reported discrete negative emotions are sensitive to change in negative emotion.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of improved measures for detecting changes in negative emotion in psychological research.

the question whether the self-report measures of the Positive and Negative affect schedule (Watson et al., 1988) are sensitive enough to detect changes in self-reported emotion that are expected to occur following manipulations designed to elicit emotional responses.
the question of how to measure the emotional impact of a given event, and how to measure the impact of that event on a given person.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the authors found that using a measure that combines discrete emotions and instructions asking participants to report their emotions after a manipulation is less sensitive to detecting changes in negative emotions than using a measure of discrete emotions and asking participants to report on how they felt during the manipulation.

The present study is an attempt to investigate the effect of the positive and negative affect schedule (PANAS) on the detection of transient emotional responses with the help of improved self-report measures.
the PANAS is a valid and reliable instrument, but it has limitations in that it measures general affect rather than discrete emotions, and that the instructions for use should be modified.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the PANAS is a poor tool for measuring discrete emotions.
we found that self-reported negative affect is more likely to be detected when participants are instructed to report how it feels to experience an emotion rather than how it feels afterward.
our work is about how to detect emotional responses in psychological research.
The main takeaway from our work is that

we can detect transient emotional responses more sensitively when we use discrete emotions rather than a measure that combines discrete emotions, and if we instruct participants to report how they feel during the event versus after it.
it’s important to use the right measure to detect emotional responses.
